title: Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: Comment
research_question: Did the April 1992 increase in New Jersey's minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour reduce employment at fast-food restaurants in the state relative to neighboring Pennsylvania, where the minimum wage was unchanged? More broadly, does raising the minimum wage decrease the demand for low-wage labor in the fast-food industry?
data_description: The authors assemble administrative payroll records from a sample of Burger King, Wendy's, Roy Rogers, and Kentucky Fried Chicken restaurants located in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania, drawn from the same chains and zip-code areas covered by Card and Krueger's (1994) telephone survey. The unit of observation is the individual restaurant, and the key variable is total nonmanagement payroll hours, converted to full-time-equivalent employees by dividing weekly hours by 35. Data cover pay periods spanning February–March 1992 (before the New Jersey minimum-wage increase) and November–December 1992 (eight to nine months after). The final sample contains 235 restaurants across 25 zip-code areas. The authors also use Card and Krueger's original telephone-survey data and BLS-790 and ES-202 state and county employment series for eating and drinking places (SIC 58) covering 1982–1996.
institutional_context: On April 1, 1991, the federal minimum wage rose to $4.25, the prevailing floor in both New Jersey and Pennsylvania. One year later, on April 1, 1992, New Jersey raised its state minimum wage to $5.05 per hour, an 18.8 percent increase, while Pennsylvania's minimum remained at $4.25. This geographic and temporal divergence between two adjacent states with otherwise similar labor markets created a widely studied policy setting for assessing how a binding wage floor affects employment in low-wage industries such as fast food, where a high share of workers earn at or near the minimum. The original Card–Krueger study of this episode attracted substantial attention because it reported that employment in New Jersey fast-food restaurants did not fall, and possibly rose, relative to Pennsylvania, contradicting the conventional competitive labor-demand prediction and influencing subsequent minimum-wage policy debates.
